case_name: Kiss et al. v. Phil Dennis Enterprises Ltd. et al.
text:
Kiss et al. v. Phil Dennis Enterprises Ltd. et al.

(1974), 3 O.R. (2d) 576

ONTARIO

HIGH COURT OF JUSTICE

WEATHERSTON, J.

9TH APRIL 1974

Planning legislation -- Zoning -- Non-conforming use -- Defendant's building on part of its lot legal non-conforming use -- Remaining part of lot zoned to prevent proposed construction of industrial building -- Driveway to proposed building running over that part of lot used as non-conforming use -- Whether defendant entitled to construct new building as part of non-conforming use -- Whether driveway part of non- conforming use.
Planning legislation -- Zoning -- Non-conforming use -- Discontinuance -- Defendant's building, a legal non- conforming use, destroyed in part by fire -- Building repaired and used throughout time repairs carried out -- Whether non-conforming use discontinued -- Planning Act, s. 35(7).
In 1958, a township which was subsequently annexed to the defendant municipality zoned the subject lands as rural agricultural, a designation which permitted industrial uses. In 1958, predecessors of the defendant corporation erected a building on the lands and carried on an industrial use. In 1967, a fire destroyed part of the building but some work continued in the undamaged portion until repairs were carried out. In 1962, part of the lands were rezoned rural residential which prohibited industrial uses. Thereafter the defendants sought and obtained a building permit to erect a second plant, which was an entity in itself on that part of the lands still zoned rural agricultural. The driveway from the proposed second building was to run across that part of the land zoned rural residential. The plaintiffs whose lands joined those of the defendant company, sought a declaration that the building permit was invalid and an injunction restraining the defendant from using the lands for the purposes intended.
Held, the plaintiffs were entitled to the declaration and the injunction sought. In 1962, when the rural residential by-law was passed the defendants had established a legal non- conforming use pursuant to s. 35(7) of the Planning Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 349, with respect to that part of its lands upon which its building stood. This use was not discontinued because of the fire and subsequent repairs resulting therefrom in 1967. Moreover, the bona fide non-conforming use of part of the lands or buildings extended to the whole parcel of land or the entire building. That part of the lands of the defendant company over which the driveway was to be built had been used for industrial purposes and the proposed change, i.e., the construction of the driveway, was one of degree and not of a kind of use. However, the whole of the defendant's lands were a lot and that lot was a residential lot by virtue of the passing of the rural residential by-law. The continuance of the existing building and use depended entirely upon s. 35(7) of the Planning Act except as to any variance, enlargement or extension of the building, or change in use that might be authorized by the committee of adjustment. The existing building was a main building and the proposed building was also to be a main building since it was to be an entity in itself. Since the rural residential by-law prohibited the erection of more than one main building on any residential lot the defendant corporation was not entitled to a building permit.
ACTION for a declaration that a building permit issued by the defendant municipality was invalid and for an injunction restraining the defendant corporation from using its lands in accordance with the building permit.

[Pickering Township v. Godfrey,
1958 CanLII 95 (ON CA)
, [1958] O.R. 429, 14 D.L.R. (2d) 520; Central Jewish Institute v. City of Toronto,
1948 CanLII 3 (SCC)
, [1948] S.C.R. 101, [1948] 2 D.L.R. 1, refd to]

R.T. Anderson, for plaintiffs.
E.A. Blackadder, for defendants, Phil Dennis Enterprises Ltd.
and Phil Dennis.
J.F. Swayze, Q.C., for defendant, City of Welland.

WEATHERSTON, J.:-- This is an action for a declaration that a
building permit issued by the building inspector for the City
of Welland to the defendant Phil Dennis Enterprises Ltd. is
invalid, and for an injunction restraining the said defendant
from using its lands as it intends to do if the building is
erected.

The lands of the plaintiffs, on which a private residence has
been erected, adjoin those of the defendant Phil Dennis
Enterprises Ltd. on the south side of the concession road
between the fourth and fifth concessions of the former Township
of Crowland, generally known as East Main St. By the Regional
Municipality of Niagara Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 406, that part of
the Township of Crowland was annexed to the City of Welland,
and by s. 18 of the Municipal Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 284, the
zoning by-laws of the township remained in force.

By-law 1538 of the Township of Crowland was passed on May 6,
1958, and, as amended by By-law 1589, was duly approved by the
Ontario Municipal Board. By that amended by-law, all of the
lands of the plaintiffs and of the defendant Phil Dennis
Enterprises Ltd. were zoned rural agricultural. The only
subsequent amendment which is relevant is By-law 1760 passed on
March 26, 1962, by which the front 300 ft. on the south side of
East Main St. was rezoned rural residential first density
(RR1). The permitted uses in a rural agricultural district
included:

7.1.2. Industrial:

A warehouse or distributing depot

Light manufacturing or assembly of manufactured products

Heavy industrial.

The only permitted use in a rural residential district (RR1),
is a private detached dwelling.

In 1959 while the land was still zoned rural agricultural,
the predecessors of the defendant Phil Dennis Enterprises Ltd.
erected a building and commenced an industrial process
described as heat treatment. This involved the heating of heavy
metal objects and then cooling them under controlled conditions
so as to change the quality of the metal. The plant was
expanded at least once before 1962. As the plant was located
entirely within 300 ft. from East Main St., its right to
continue in operation after the passing of By-law 1760 depended
upon s. 30(7) of the Planning Act, R.S.O. 1960, c. 296 (now
R.S.O. 1970, c. 349, s. 35(7)), as follows:

35(7) No by-law passed under this section applies,

(a) to prevent the use of any land, building or structure
for any purpose prohibited by the by-law if such
land, building or structure was lawfully used for
such purpose on the day of the passing of the by-law,
so long as it continues to be used for that purpose;

Applications for minor variances so as to permit enlargements
of the existing building were granted by the committee of
adjustment in 1967 and in 1969. A further application by the
defendant Phil Dennis Enterprises Ltd. was refused on February
14, 1973. The defendant Phil Dennis Enterprises Ltd. then
applied for and on February 28, 1973, was granted a building
permit "to erect a heat treat plant 50' x 100'0" of masonry
const. and steel frame. The proposed building to have a front
yard setback of 307'0" plus from front property line left side
yard 56'7" and right side yard 43'5" and rear yard 200'0" plus
as per plan and application filed".

It was conceded by Mr. Dennis in evidence that this building
would be independent of the existing building and "an entity in
itself".

The plaintiffs claim that the building permit ought not to
have been granted and that the defendant is not entitled to
erect the building because:

1. the non-conforming use of the land was discontinued after a
fire in 1967;

2. the proposed driveway leading from East Main St. to the new
building is a new or extended use not permitted in a rural
residential zone, and

3. under the by-law only one main building is permitted.

The fire in 1967 was undoubtedly a serious fire, but the
entire building was not demolished, the work crew was not laid
off, and in fact some work continued in an undamaged portion of
the building.

At its meeting on August 28, 1967, the Council of the
Township of Crowland passed a resolution "that the application
of H & S Heat Treating Limited to restore the building that was
partially destroyed by fire be approved and that a building
permit be issued". A building permit was issued on September
25, 1967, "to restore shop (repair and re-roof)". In my
opinion, the use of the building as a heat treatment plant was
not discontinued during repair. There was a continuing
intention to use the building for its intended purpose, and an
actual user for that purpose so far as was possible at the
time: Re Hartley and City of Toronto
(1925), 56 O.L.R. 433 at
p. 435
; City of Toronto v. Board of Trustees of R.C. Separate
Schools for City of Toronto,
1925 CanLII 326 (UK JCPC)
, [1925] 3 D.L.R. 880 at p. 884,
[1926] A.C. 81.

By-laws 1538 and 1760 were passed under the authority of what
is now s. 35(1) of the Planning Act:

1. For prohibiting the use of land, for or except for such
purposes as may be set out in the by-law within the
municipality or within any defined area or areas or
abutting on any defined highway or part of a highway.

2. For prohibiting the erection or use of buildings or
structures for or except for such purposes as may be set
out in the by-law within the municipality or within any
defined area or areas or upon land abutting on any defined
highway or part of a highway.

These two classes of property are dealt with together in s. 5
of the by-law, which provides:

5.1 Scope

No person shall, within any district of the Township of
Crowland, use any land or erect or use any building or
structure except in conformity with the provisions of
this By-law.

5.2 Non-conforming uses

Nothing in this By-law shall apply to any land, building
or structure which, on the day of the passing of this By-
law, is lawfully used or erected for any purpose
prohibited by this By-law, as long as it continues to be
used for that purpose, nor shall this By-law apply to any
building or structure the plans for which have been
approved by the building inspector prior to the day of
the passing of this By-law, so long as the building or
structure, when erected, is used for the purpose for
which it was erected, and provided the erection of such
building or structure is commenced within two years after
the day of the passing of this By-law and such building
or structure is completed within a reasonable time after
the erection thereof is commenced.

There is no doubt that the lands at the rear, on which the
proposed building is to be erected, may be used for their
intended industrial purpose. The only question is whether
traffic coming and going from East Main St. to that building
will be a continuance of the lawful non-conforming use of the
lands zoned RR1 or whether it will be a different use. The
answer to that question depends upon whether the present use of
the lands is a "use" of the entire parcel for the industrial
purposes now concentrated in the existing building. lt is a
fact that the area over which the driveway is to be built was
not actively used, but had been landscaped, and trees and grass
had been planted.

In Pickering Township v. Godfrey,
1958 CanLII 95 (ON CA)
, [1958] O.R. 429, 14 D.L.R.
(2d) 520, the question was whether the extraction of gravel
was a "use" of land. Morden, J.A., giving the main judgment of
the Court, said at p. 437 O.R., pp. 524-5 D.L.R.:

Counsel did not refer to any decisions interpreting the
words "use of land" as they appear in s. 390 and I could find
none. The dictionary definitions of "use" are numerous and
diverse. An examination of them and some authorities, to
which I will refer, has led me to the opinion that the word
when used in conjunction with such commodities as food and
water connotes the idea of consumption, but when applied to
more durable forms of property means the employment of the
property for enjoyment, revenue or profit without in any way
otherwise diminishing or impairing the property itself. For
example, in the Civil Law, usufruct is defined as "the power
of disposal of the use and fruits, saving the substance of
the thing": Stair's Institutes, (1681) xvi, p. 327. The same
distinction was made by Falconbridge, J., in Re Davis v.
Toronto
(1892), 21 O.R. 243
in interpreting another section
of the Municipal Act. At p. 247, he is reported as saying:
--

"'Using' applied to land cannot mean wasting, consuming
or exhausting by employment, as, e.g. to use flour, beer,
or water, for food or drink. It means holding or
occupying, and so must be read with the rest of the
section, ..."

Central Jewish Institute v. City of Toronto,
1948 CanLII 3 (SCC)
, [1948] S.C.R.
101, [1948] 2 D.L.R. 1, involved the question whether the
appellant had established a "use" of a building as a school
prior to the passing of a by-law prohibiting such a use. A
number of children and three teachers went on the property on
July 15, 1946, and from then until the by-law was passed on
July 24, 1946, the grounds and part of the building were used
by teachers and children as a nursery school for very young
children. The trial Judge and Court of Appeal proceeded on the
ground that the principal use of the premises on the date the
by-law was passed, was as a residence and guest house, and that
a lawful non-conforming use as a school had not therefore been
established. Kerwin, J., at p. 106 S.C.R., p. 5 D.L.R., said:

It actually used the premises as a school and the mere fact
that it was a nursery summer school does not prevent the
appellant increasing the number of pupils or enlarging the
scope of its activities so as to conduct classes not in
operation at the relevant time.

Rand, J., said at p. 109 S.C.R., p. 8 D.L.R.:

It will be seen that the exemption is not to the existing
use but to the building; and there is no implication that it
is the whole of the building that must be so used or that the
use must be the sole use. The language would be satisfied by
a partial use as if, for instance, an owner was carrying on a
grocery store on the ground floor and using the second storey
for his home: could it seriously be questioned that the use
of the lower floor in such a case would be protected by the
exemption? If that same business were extended to the upper
storey, could it be said that the exemption did not continue
or was lost? The building would still be used on the ground
floor for the prohibited purpose; the building as a whole
would be exempt; and I think it would necessarily follow that
no such extension could bring about a forfeiture of the
exemption. In any case the question is whether a real use, in
good faith, is being made of the building, a use not merely
incidental to some other use, but possessing an individuality
of its own.

I deduce therefore that a bona fide use of any part of the
lands or buildings extends to the whole parcel of land or the
entire building. I am confirmed in this opinion by s. 42 [am.
1971, Vol. 2, c. 2, s. 5; 1972, c. 118, s. 10], of the Planning
Act by which the committee of adjustment may authorize a minor
variance from the provisions of the by-law "in respect of the
land, building or structure or the use thereof", or permit the
enlargement or extension of a building or structure or permit a
change in the use of the land to one more compatible with the
permitted uses. It will be noted that there is no provision for
the extension of a use to a different part of the land,
building or structure. It follows therefore that that part of
the lands of Phil Dennis Enterprises Ltd. over which the
driveway is to be built has been used for industrial purposes,
and that the proposed change is one of degree, and not of kind
of use.

The next question is whether the by-law prohibits the
erection of the proposed building, even though the building is
to be erected on lands which may be used for industrial
purposes.

The lands have a frontage of 200 ft. on East Main St. by a
depth of 635 ft. All counsel are agreed that this parcel of
land is a "lot" within the meaning of the by-law. Moreover, in
my view, it is a residential lot.

The following sections of the by-law are relevant:

2.50 "Lot" shall mean a parcel of land fronting on a street
whether or not occupied by a building or structure:

2.55 "Lot Residential" shall mean a lot situated in a
residential district and having a lot frontage and lot area
in accordance with the requirements of the district in which
the same is situated;

5.24 Residential District

Wherein this By-law the term "Residential District" is used,
it shall include the following Districts: Rural Agricultural
(RA), Rural Residential First Density (RR1), Rural
Residential Second Density (RR2), Private Detached Dwelling
First Density (R1), Private Detached Dwelling Second Density
(R2), Private Detached Dwelling Third Density (R3),
Multiple-Family Dwelling, First Density (RM1) and Multiple-
Family Dwelling, Second Density (RM2), unless the contrary
intention appears.

6.1 Residential Lot Occupancy

No person shall erect more than one main building on any
Residential lot.

The following provisions of the by-law relate to accessory
buildings:

2.1 "Accessory" when used to describe a building or structure
shall mean a detached subordinate building or structure, not
used for human habitation, located on the same lot with the
main building; and when used to describe a use shall mean a
use customarily incidental and subordinate to and located on
the same lot as the principal use of the premises.

5.6 Obstruction of Yards

No person shall obstruct in any manner whatsoever any front
yard, side yard or rear yard required to be provided by this
By-law, but this provision shall not apply to:

. . . . .

(f) accessory buildings permitted by this By-law.

5.14 Accessory Uses

Wherein this By-law a use is permitted, accessory buildings
and accessory use thereto shall also be permitted.

5.15.5 Accessory Use:

No accessory building shall be used for any purpose other
than a use that is incidental or secondary to that of the
main building on the same lot and without limiting the
foregoing such use may include a private garage, recreation
building, greenhouse or bath house if not used for commercial
purposes.

I do not consider that the provisions of the by-law relating
to accessory buildings are material to the questions in issue
in this action. The use made of the front 300 ft. is not a
permitted use, and therefore "accessory buildings and accessory
use thereto" are not permitted. The continuance of the existing
building and use depends entirely on s. 35(7) of the Planning
Act, except as to any variance, enlargement or extension of the
building, or change in use authorized by the committee of
adjustment. The existing building is certainly a "main
building", and the proposed building is also a "main building"
since it is to be "an entity in itself". Therefore, it is not
permitted by s. 6.1 of the by-law, and the building permit
ought not to have been issued.

The plaintiffs are entitled to a declaration that the
building permit ought not to have been issued, and to an order
enjoining the defendant Phil Dennis Enterprises Ltd. from
erecting a building in conformity therewith. No case was made
out against the defendant Phil Dennis, and the action against
him will be dismissed without costs.

The plaintiffs are entitled to their costs against the other
two defendants.

Judgment accordingly.
